# 2 Chronicles 6:22–42 — Verse-by-Verse Commentary

## Overview of the Structure

Solomon's dedicatory prayer includes **seven specific situations** for which he asks God to hear prayers from heaven (Constable). The Pulpit Commentary identifies them as: (1) the man wronged by his neighbour (vv. 22–23); (2) the people defeated by enemies (vv. 24–25); (3) the people suffering drought (vv. 26–27); (4) the people visited by famine, plague or calamity (vv. 28–31); (5) the foreigner who comes to pray (vv. 32–33); (6) the people going to war (vv. 34–35); (7) the people in captivity (vv. 36–39). The prayer then closes (vv. 40–42).
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/2-chronicles-6.html

---

## v. 22 — The Oath Before the Altar

**Traditional reading:** This verse envisions a case where a man is accused of wronging his neighbour (e.g., a property dispute or a deposit left for safekeeping) and no witnesses are available. The accused is then required to take a solemn oath of self-purgation before the altar in the temple. The practice is rooted in Exodus 22:9–11 and Leviticus 6:1–5, where an oath before the LORD settled cases that human judges could not resolve. The "oath" was effectively a curse the swearer called down upon himself if his denial proved false.
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/2_chronicles/6-22.htm (Cambridge Bible, Ellicott, Pulpit Commentary)
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/2_chronicles/6-22.htm (Barnes)

**JFB adds:** In cases where testimony could not be obtained, the practice had acquired the force of consuetudinary law — the party was brought before the altar, where the oath was taken with full solemnity and a curse imprecated upon himself should his disavowal be found untrue.
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jfb/2_chronicles/6.htm

**David Guzik notes:** The temple grounds were used as a place to verify and authorise oaths. When a dispute came down to one word against another, Solomon asked that the temple would be a place to properly swear by.
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-chronicles-6/

---

## v. 23 — God as the Judge Who Sees the Heart

**Traditional reading:** Solomon asked God to "hear from heaven and act" — to judge His servants. The appeal is that God would bring retribution on the wicked by causing his own false oath to recoil upon his head, while vindicating ("justifying") the righteous by rewarding him according to his innocence. This is the first of seven occurrences of the refrain "hear from heaven" in the prayer (vv. 23, 25, 27, 30, 33, 35, 39).
— https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-chronicles-6-commentary

**Guzik:** Solomon asked the God who can see what man cannot — who knows the hidden heart of man — to enforce from heaven the oaths made at the temple. The old Puritan commentator John Trapp recorded a striking claimed fulfilment: "Anne Averies, who, forswearing herself, A.D. 1575, February 11, at a shop of Wood Street in London, praying God she might sink where she stood if she had not paid for the wares she took, fell down presently speechless, and with horrible stink died."
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-chronicles-6/

**Matthew Henry:** "That God would give judgment according to equity upon all the appeals that should be made to him … This we may, in faith, pray for, for we are sure it shall be done. God sitteth on the throne judging right."
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mhcw/2_chronicles/6.htm

---

## vv. 24–25 — Defeat Before an Enemy

**Traditional reading:** Israel's military defeats were understood covenantally — they occurred "because they have sinned against You" (see Deuteronomy 28:25). Solomon did not ask for automatic victory but for God to hear when a defeated, humbled Israel returned to Him, confessed His name, and prayed in the temple. The petition is for both forgiveness and restoration to the land. God answered this prayer repeatedly in Israel's history.
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-chronicles-6/

**Ligonier (Reformed perspective):** The prayer focuses "particularly on prayers prompted by God's discipline that could come in the form of military defeat, famine, drought, or exile (see Deut. 28:15–68). Praying toward the temple was a tangible way that the people focused their attention on the Lord."
— https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/solomons-prayer-of-dedication

**Precept Austin cites the parallel:** Joshua 7:5 is the classic example — defeat at Ai because of Achan's sin, followed by repentance and eventual restoration.
— https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-chronicles-6-commentary

---

## vv. 26–27 — Drought and the "Good Way"

**Traditional reading:** In an agricultural economy, drought ("the heavens are shut up") was a covenantal curse (Deuteronomy 28:23–24). Solomon assumes drought comes "because Your people have sinned against You." The remedy is threefold: (1) pray toward the temple, (2) confess God's name, and (3) turn from sin. Notably, Solomon says "because You have afflicted them" — recognising God's hand in the drought as chastisement designed to produce repentance. The goal is not merely rain but that God would "teach them the good way in which they should walk."
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-chronicles-6/

**Matthew Henry:** The prayer teaches "what things to mind and desire most in our prayers … First and chiefly, he prays for repentance and forgiveness, which is the chief blessing, and the only solid foundation of other mercies."
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/2_chronicles/6-22.htm

---

## vv. 28–31 — Plague, Famine, and Individual Prayer

**Traditional reading:** Solomon broadens the scope to any calamity — famine, pestilence, blight, mildew, locusts, grasshoppers, siege, or "whatever plague or sickness." The prayer opens to individual petitioners: "each knowing his own afflictions and spreading out his hands toward this temple."

**v. 30** contains a crucial theological truth: God repays each according to his ways "since You know his heart — for You alone know the hearts of men." This affirms God's unique ability to judge justly because He alone knows the inner person. It also echoes Jeremiah 17:10.

**v. 31:** The ultimate purpose of answered prayer is doxological and pedagogical — "so that they may fear You and walk in Your ways all the days they live in the land." Forgiveness is not an end in itself but leads to transformed living.
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-chronicles-6/
— https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-chronicles-6-commentary

**Guzik cites Spurgeon:** "It is not therefore to be wondered at that, when Solomon dedicated to the Lord the temple which he had built, his great petition was that God would hear every prayer that should be uttered in that place or toward that place. He wished the temple always to be to Israel the token that God's memorial is that he hears prayer."
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-chronicles-6/

---

## vv. 32–33 — The Foreigner Who Prays

**Traditional reading:** This is widely regarded as one of the most remarkable features of Solomon's prayer. The temple was in Israel but was always intended to be "a house of prayer for all nations" (Isaiah 56:7). The foreigner comes "from a distant land because of Your great name and Your mighty hand and outstretched arm" — drawn by God's reputation, not by ethnic heritage.

**Guzik:** "Solomon asked God to hear the prayer of the foreigner out of a missionary impulse. He knew that when God mercifully answered the prayers of foreigners, it drew those from other nations to the God of all nations."
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-chronicles-6/

**Selman (cited by Guzik):** "What is especially notable is that foreigners could know and fear God 'like your people Israel.' This hope of equality in worship was rarely expressed in the Old Testament (e.g. Genesis 12:3; Isaiah 19:24–25; Zechariah 8:20–22), and even Jesus' closest disciples found its fulfillment hard to take (Acts 10:1–11:18)."
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-chronicles-6/

**Guzik adds:** Jesus' cleansing of the temple (Matthew 21:13) was prompted by the violation of this very principle — the court of the Gentiles, the only place where non-Israelites could pray, had been turned into a marketplace.
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-chronicles-6/

---

## vv. 34–35 — Going Out to War

**Traditional reading:** Solomon carefully conditions this petition: the people go to war "wherever You send them." This is not a blanket request for divine blessing on every military campaign but specifically on those undertaken at God's direction. The prayer is that when the soldiers face the direction of Jerusalem and the temple and pray, God would "uphold their cause" (literally, "do their judgment" or "maintain their right").
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-chronicles-6/

**Constable:** This is the sixth of seven situations Solomon specified for divine intervention in answer to prayer.
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/2-chronicles-6.html

---

## vv. 36–39 — Sin, Exile, and Repentance

**v. 36 — "For there is no one who does not sin":** This is one of the Old Testament's clearest statements of the universality of sin, foreshadowing Romans 3:23. Solomon does not say "if they sin" but "when they sin," because sin is inevitable for fallen humanity.
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-chronicles-6/

**Selman (cited by Guzik):** "The sense that sin is all-pervading dominates, epitomised in one of the clearest biblical statements about sin's universality … No greater indication of the need for a place of atonement and forgiveness could be given."
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-chronicles-6/

**v. 37 — "When they come to their senses":** The Hebrew concept involves a turning point of realisation. The confession is threefold: "We have sinned and done wrong; we have acted wickedly" — a comprehensive admission of guilt covering the act, the wrongness, and the moral rebellion.

**v. 38 — "Return to You with all their heart and soul":** The repentance must be wholehearted (cf. Deuteronomy 30:1–10). Even in a foreign land, prayer is directed "in the direction of the land … the city … the house" — the spatial orientation symbolising spiritual orientation toward God's covenant promises.

**v. 39 — The petition:** That God would hear, forgive, and uphold their cause. This anticipates the eventual return from exile under Ezra and Nehemiah.
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-chronicles-6/

**Ligonier (Reformed):** "The king knew that having the temple was no guarantee that God would continue to bless Israel if they fell into gross sin, but He also knew that the Lord would show grace if the people turned from their sin and trusted in Him anew. Even when Israel grossly sinned, He would not forget His covenant."
— https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/solomons-prayer-of-dedication

**Constable:** The seventh and final situation — captivity due to sin — recognizes that "God could answer prayers made away from the temple," affirming God's transcendence while the temple was the focal point of His immanence.
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/2-chronicles-6.html

### Where Protestant traditions differ on v. 36

The statement "there is no one who does not sin" touches on the doctrine of total depravity and the universality of sin. Reformed and Lutheran traditions cite this alongside Romans 3:23 and Psalm 51:5 as biblical evidence that all humans inherit a sinful nature from Adam and are incapable of not sinning apart from grace. Arminian and Wesleyan traditions affirm the universality of sin but differ on the extent of its effect; they hold that prevenient grace restores the ability to choose God, and that sanctification can bring believers to a state where they may cease from wilful sin (though not from all error). The verse itself, however, states a universal negative — "there is no one who does not sin" — which both sides affirm as describing the general human condition.

The StudyLight.org verse-by-verse page for 2 Chronicles 6:36 notes that among contributors, the theological stance is recorded as 7 Calvinist, 7 Arminian, 11 Dispensationalist, and 2 Lutheran — indicating broad agreement on the verse's plain sense.
— https://www.studylight.org/commentary/2-chronicles/6-36.html

**Grant's Commentary (Dispensational):** Sees vv. 36–39 as prophetic of Israel's future: "There is no shadow of doubt that Israel will do this eventually … The Great Tribulation will eventually break down their arrogant pride to make such a confession as is seen in verse 37."
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/lmg/2-chronicles-6.html

---

## vv. 40–42 — The Conclusion of the Prayer

**v. 40 — "Now, my God, may Your eyes be open and Your ears attentive":** A summary plea echoing verse 20. Solomon asks for God's continuing attentiveness to prayers offered in the temple.

**v. 41 — "Arise, O LORD God, and enter Your resting place":** This is the section unique to Chronicles (not found in 1 Kings 8). Solomon draws on the language of Numbers 10:35–36 — the words Moses spoke when the ark set out and when it rested during the wilderness wanderings. Now the ark has found its permanent "resting place." The phrase "You and the ark of Your might" indicates that the ark was the visible symbol of God's powerful presence.
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-chronicles-6/

**JFB:** "'Arise' is a very suitable expression to be used when the ark was to be removed from the tabernacle in Zion to the temple on Mount Moriah … The ark of thy strength — the abode by which Thy glorious presence is symbolized, and whence Thou dost issue Thine authoritative oracles, and manifest Thy power on behalf of Thy people."
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jfb/2_chronicles/6.htm

**Keil & Delitzsch:** The phrase "arise into Thy rest" is not inconsistent with the ark already being in the Holy of Holies; the verb קוּמָה (qumah) has the general sense of "set oneself to something." The idea is that God would now occupy His throne as the God of salvation.
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/2_chronicles/6-22.htm (Keil & Delitzsch section)

**"Let Your priests be clothed with salvation":** JFB explains this means the priests should be "equipped not only with the pure white linen garments … but also adorned with the moral beauties of true holiness, that their person and services may be accepted." Their being "clothed with salvation" is the effect and consequence of a sanctified character.
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jfb/2_chronicles/6.htm

**"Let Your godly ones rejoice in goodness":** The saints (hasidim, the covenant-faithful) are to find their joy in God's goodness manifested through the temple worship.

**v. 42 — "Do not reject Your anointed one":** Solomon refers to himself as the LORD's anointed king. "Turn not away the face" is an idiom for denying a request (see 1 Kings 2:16).
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/2_chronicles/6-42.htm (search excerpt — Ellicott, Pulpit Commentary)

**Guzik:** "Solomon probably meant this in reference to himself because he was the anointed king of Israel. Nevertheless, it also reminds us of the principle in prayer of praying in the name of Jesus, the ultimate Anointed One." Payne adds: "In his prayer 'do not reject your anointed one,' the king now meant himself, though in subsequent usage it would express Israel's hope in the coming Messiah."
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-chronicles-6/

**"Remember Your loving devotion to Your servant David":** Literally "the mercies (ḥasadim) of David." JFB explains these are "the mercies promised to David, and in consideration of that promise, hear and answer my prayer (cf. Psalm 132:10)." Keil & Delitzsch notes a different nuance — the "pious deeds of David" — all that David did for the advancement of public worship.
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jfb/2_chronicles/6.htm
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/2_chronicles/6-22.htm (Keil & Delitzsch)

**Matthew Henry (Christological reading):** "Lord, remember his merits, and accept of us on the account of them. Remember the promises of the everlasting covenant, which are called the sure mercies of David, Isaiah 55:3. This must be all our desire, all our hope, all our prayer, and all our plea; for it is all our salvation."
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/2_chronicles/6-42.htm (search excerpt — Matthew Henry)

**The Matthew Henry Concise Commentary** offers a strongly Christological reading of the entire prayer: "The temple typified the human nature of Christ, in whom dwelleth all the fulness of the Godhead bodily. The ark typified his obedience and sufferings, by which repenting sinners have access to a reconciled God … May the Father look upon us in and through his Anointed."
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/2_chronicles/6-22.htm

## Summary of the Seven-Fold "Hear from Heaven"

Precept Austin notes the seven-fold refrain: "hear from heaven" appears at vv. 23, 25, 27, 30, 33, 35, and 39 — each time linked to a different situation of need and prayer.
— https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-chronicles-6-commentary

The prayer moves from individual disputes (v. 22–23), to national defeat (v. 24–25), to natural disaster (v. 26–27), to general calamity and individual affliction (v. 28–31), to the foreigner seeking God (v. 32–33), to war (v. 34–35), and finally to the most extreme case — national exile because of sin (v. 36–39). The structure demonstrates that no circumstance lies beyond the reach of prayer or divine forgiveness.

## Modern Scholarship

The NET Bible notes were referenced by Precept Austin for v. 5: "Here 'name' is used by metonymy for the LORD himself, and thus the expression 'to be there' refers to his taking up residence there." This "name theology" is important in the Chronicler's understanding of the temple.
— https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-chronicles-6-commentary

Constable notes that the Chronicler wrote when the second temple's legitimacy was being contested (Ezra 4:4–24; Haggai 1:2–4), and that Solomon's prayer served to validate the temple as the place where God had placed His name and where the returned exiles could obey the laws of expiation, worship, and fellowship with God.
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/2-chronicles-6.html
